name: Kinesiology tape posture taping

lead: Posture taping means sticking elastic kinesiology tape across the shoulders and upper back so you feel a tug when your shoulders slump. People use it as a reminder to hold the shoulders back, aiming for less rounded shoulders and forward head and a better side profile and neck line.

The chain is a tactile cue, shoulders held back, then a better profile. The tape was developed in the 1970s by Kenzo Kase and became widely visible at the 2008 and 2012 Olympics. Systematic reviews of it for pain and performance report small effects, and no controlled trial of tape as a posture method for appearance was found.

paras: Strips are applied across the upper back and shoulders and worn for days at a time, often during desk work or training. Proponents describe it as feedback that improves body awareness while worn, and many pair it with posture exercises.

Skin irritation from the adhesive is the main general concern. Manufacturers have also made claims about fascia and lymph flow that critics say lack evidence, and in 2017 the leading brand settled a lawsuit over marketing claims.

angle.text: People tape the upper back with elastic tape as a reminder to hold the shoulders back, aiming for a better profile and neck line. The path runs from a tug cue to shoulders held back to less rounded posture. Research on the tape concerns pain; its use for posture appearance has not been tested.

lead: Kinesiology tape posture taping is the use of stretchy, adhesive elastic tape, commonly sold as Kinesio tape or K-tape, across the shoulders and upper back to cue a more upright shoulder position. People use it to counter rounded shoulders and forward-head posture, which they associate with a broader-looking upper body, a more open chest and a cleaner side profile and neck line.[1]

The tape is a thin cotton strip with acrylic adhesive that can stretch to roughly 140 percent of its length. It was developed in the 1970s by Kenzo Kase, a Japanese-American chiropractor, and became widely visible after it was supplied to athletes at the 2008 and 2012 Olympics.[1]

Unlike most uses of the tape, posture taping has been studied directly. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of nine randomized trials with 293 participants found that taping groups differed significantly from controls on forward shoulder angle but not on craniovertebral angle or pain, and the authors noted that the evidence quality is low.[2] A 2024 double-blind trial in 114 people with rounded shoulders and shoulder impingement reported posture improvements over sham taping immediately after application.[3]

paras: Kinesiology tape is a latex-free elastic cotton tape with a heat-activated acrylic adhesive, designed to approximate the thickness and elasticity of skin. When applied under stretch it recoils and tugs gently on the skin.[1]

For posture, practitioners and users apply strips across the upper back or shoulder blades so that the tape tension is felt when the shoulders round forward, intended as a sensory reminder rather than a mechanical brace.

Kenzo Kase developed the tape in the 1970s and his company sells it under the Kinesio brand. Its popularity rose after the product was donated to athletes at the 2008 Beijing and 2012 London Olympics, and beach volleyball player Kerri Walsh wearing it on her shoulder in 2008 is often cited as a visible moment.[1]

In 2017 the company KT Health settled a Massachusetts class action over its marketing for 1.75 million US dollars, agreeing to refunds and to drop claims such as injury prevention while adding a disclaimer that the tape was not clinically proven for all injuries.[1]

Manufacturers and users have proposed that the tape lifts the skin to decompress fascia, improves lymphatic flow, reduces pressure on pain receptors, or improves proprioception, meaning the awareness of body position. Critics cited by Wikipedia say these claims lack supporting evidence.[1] The proprioception-cue explanation is the one most aligned with posture use.

For posture specifically, a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of Musculoskeletal Research (Niranjan, Harikesavan and Kalyan) included nine randomized trials with 293 participants with upper-quadrant postural dysfunction. Taping was associated with a significant difference in forward shoulder angle, with no significant difference in craniovertebral angle or pain; the authors cautioned that evidence quality was low.[2]

A 2024 randomized, double-blind trial in Medicine (Demircioglu and Genc) assigned 114 people with rounded shoulder posture and subacromial impingement to Kinesio taping or sham taping. Taping reduced pain, improved proprioception in abduction and improved posture on the New York Posture Rating Chart (P =.040) immediately after application; effects beyond that were not examined.[3]

Reviews of the tape for other purposes include a 2012 finding of trivial pain relief in sports injuries, a 2014 finding of negligible effect on muscle strength, and a 2015 finding of benefit over no treatment, but not over other treatments, for chronic musculoskeletal pain.[1] A 2026 meta-analysis reported significant pain reduction in patellofemoral pain syndrome, while a 2021 review found no strong evidence for pain relief in knee osteoarthritis.[4][5]
As with any skin adhesive, skin irritation is a general consideration; the trials above do not describe adverse effects in detail.
